title: PostgreSQL DBA Part 6: pg_hba.conf and Client Authentication
description: Learn pg_hba.conf on PostgreSQL 18 for Ubuntu: rule order, peer vs scram-sha-256, allowing remote connections, testing rules and fixing login errors.

sources.title: PostgreSQL 18 docs: 19.3 Connections and Authentication (listen_addresses, password_encryption, md5_password_warnings)
PostgreSQL 18 release notes (MD5 deprecation, oauth method)

reviewNotes: Series part 6. Part 5 is live and linked in the intro and related. Followed the PostgreSQL 18 documentation (docs/current). TESTING CAVEAT, same as Parts 4 and 5: the postgresql-18 server package still cannot be installed in this sandbox (its dependency liburing2 comes from archive.ubuntu.com, which the network policy blocks). Commands were run with psql 18.6 (postgresql-client-18 18.6-1.pgdg24.04+2) against the preinstalled PostgreSQL 16.15 server on Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS, cluster 16 main, with paths rewritten from 16 to 18. Why the outputs should match 18: I extracted the postgresql-18 18.6 .deb; its pg_hba.conf.sample is 122 lines, identical to 16's except the comment listing methods now includes "oauth", so the Ubuntu-generated file has the same rule lines and line numbers (118, 123, 125, 127, 130-132). I grepped the 18.6 postgres binary for every server message quoted: no pg_hba.conf entry for host ... %s; pg_hba.conf rejects connection ...; password authentication failed; Peer authentication failed; invalid authentication method; Connection matched file ... line; and the 18-only MD5 warning texts (setting an MD5-encrypted password / MD5 password support is deprecated... / Refer to the PostgreSQL documentation...). Blocks captioned plain 'Output' are real and path-free. Blocks captioned '(expected output)' had 16->18 in paths, and for the network tests the sandbox address 192.0.2.2 / rule 192.0.2.0/24 was replaced with the article's example 10.0.0.11 / 10.0.0.0/24; the editor should confirm on a real 18 server with a 10.0.0.x network. The MD5 CREATE ROLE warning block is not tested (16 has no warning): I assumed WARNING/DETAIL/HINT levels for the three strings; please confirm the exact layout on 18. The 'does not have a valid SCRAM secret' DETAIL text was taken from the 18.6 binary strings, not from a live test. The md5 hash prefix 'md55804793cdf4' is real and deterministic (md5 of password+username). The practice-exercise answer (10.0.0.30/24 loads with no error and shows netmask 255.255.255.0) was tested on 16 with these exact values. The sandbox has no systemd, so reloads/restarts were done with pg_ctlcluster / pg_reload_conf(); systemctl commands are shown per the series platform. On a host with IPv6, listen_addresses='*' also logs a '::' line (not seen in sandbox). The LinkedIn listen_addresses slide uses ALTER SYSTEM instead of the article's conf.d file, for brevity.

data.text: This is Part 6 of the PostgreSQL DBA series. pg_hba.conf is the file that decides who may connect to your PostgreSQL server, to which database, from which address, and how they must prove who they are. To allow remote connections you change two things: listen_addresses in postgresql.conf (so the server listens on the network) and a host line in pg_hba.conf (so the server accepts that client). By the end of this part you will be able to read every line of the default file, add a rule for an application server, test it before you reload, and fix the error messages people hit most often.
In Part 5 we covered postgresql.conf, including the difference between a reload and a restart. You will use both here: pg_hba.conf changes need only a reload, while listen_addresses needs a restart.
What you will learn

items.content: What each column of a pg_hba.conf line means, and the first-match rule
What the Ubuntu default rules do, and why sudo -u postgres psql needs no password
How to let an application server connect with scram-sha-256 passwords
How to test the file with the pg_hba_file_rules view before you reload
How to find and convert old MD5 passwords, which PostgreSQL 18 deprecates
How to read the real authentication errors and fix each one

data.text: Prerequisites

items.content: Parts 2 to 5 of this series: installing PostgreSQL 18, the data directory, psql, and postgresql.conf with reload vs restart.
One Ubuntu server with PostgreSQL 18 from the PGDG repository and cluster 18 main running (check with pg_lsclusters). In this part the server is called db1 with address 10.0.0.11.

Optional: a second machine (the application server app1, 10.0.0.21) with the PostgreSQL client installed (sudo apt-get install -y postgresql-client-18). If you have only one machine, you can test from db1 itself, as shown below.
A Linux user with sudo rights, and a test server. A wrong pg_hba.conf can lock everyone out, so practise away from production.

data.text: How it works

Think of pg_hba.conf as the guest list at the door of a building. Before anyone reaches a database, the server reads the list from the top. It looks for the first line that matches the visitor: how they arrived, which database they want, which user name they gave and where they came from. That line says how the visitor must prove their identity, or that they must be turned away.

HBA stands for host-based authentication. Authentication means proving who you are (for example with a password). It is different from authorization, which decides what you may do once you are in (GRANT and REVOKE, covered in Part 7).
Each rule is one line with these columns:

data.code:
# TYPE  DATABASE        USER            ADDRESS                 METHOD
host    shop            app_user        10.0.0.0/24             scram-sha-256
data.caption: The columns of one pg_hba.conf rule

content: local (Unix socket on the same machine), host (TCP/IP, with or without SSL), hostssl (TCP/IP with SSL only), hostnossl (TCP/IP without SSL only)
Which database the client asks for
all, a name, a comma list, sameuser, replication (physical replication connections)
Which database role the client gives
all, a role name, +groupname (any member of that role)
Where the client comes from (not used for local)
How the client proves who it is
peer, scram-sha-256, reject, trust, md5 (deprecated), cert, ldap and others

data.text: The address uses CIDR notation: an IP address, a slash and the number of fixed bits. 10.0.0.0/24 means every address from 10.0.0.0 to 10.0.0.255, and /32 means exactly one IPv4 address. Do not put spaces around the slash.
The methods you will use most:

items.content: peer: for local socket connections only. The server asks the Linux kernel which operating system user opened the connection and allows it only if that name equals the database user name. No password is involved.
scram-sha-256: password check using a challenge and response, so the password itself never travels over the network, and the server stores only a salted hash. This is the method to use for passwords.
reject: always refuse. Useful to block one host or user above a broader rule.
trust: allow anyone who matches, with no password, as any user they name. Avoid it outside a throwaway test machine.
md5: an older password method. It is deprecated in PostgreSQL 18 and will be removed in a future release.

data.text: Two rules decide everything:

items.content: First match wins. The server uses the first line whose type, database, user and address all match. If authentication on that line fails, it does not try the next line. If no line matches, the connection is refused.
The file is read at start and on reload. On Linux, editing the file does nothing until you reload the server. A reload does not disconnect anyone; existing sessions keep running.

data.text: pg_hba.conf only controls the door. A user must also have the CONNECT privilege on the database. The documentation suggests that limiting who may connect to which database is often easier with GRANT and REVOKE CONNECT than with many pg_hba.conf lines.
Reading the Ubuntu default rules
Step 1: Find the file the server is using
On db1, as your sudo user. On Ubuntu the file is not inside the data directory. Ask the server where it is, so you never edit the wrong copy:

data.code: sudo -u postgres psql -c "SHOW hba_file;"
data.caption: Show the path of pg_hba.conf

data.code:
hba_file               
-------------------------------------
 /etc/postgresql/18/main/pg_hba.conf
(1 row)
data.caption: Output (expected output: the path shows 18 on a PostgreSQL 18 server)

data.text: The file belongs to the postgres Linux user with permissions -rw-r-----, so you need sudo to read or edit it. Next to it is pg_ident.conf, which holds optional user name maps for peer and ident; you do not need it in this part.
Step 2: List the active lines
On db1, as your sudo user. The file is about 130 lines, most of them comments. Show only the real rules:

data.code: sudo grep -vE '^\s*(#|$)' /etc/postgresql/18/main/pg_hba.conf
data.caption: Show pg_hba.conf without comments and blank lines

content: Print lines that do NOT match the pattern
A line that starts (after optional spaces) with # or is empty

data.code:
local   all             postgres                                peer
local   all             all                                     peer
host    all             all             127.0.0.1/32            scram-sha-256
host    all             all             ::1/128                 scram-sha-256
local   replication     all                                     peer
host    replication     all             127.0.0.1/32            scram-sha-256
host    replication     all             ::1/128                 scram-sha-256
data.caption: Output

data.text: Read it top to bottom. Local socket connections use peer, so the Linux user postgres can log in as the database user postgres without a password. TCP connections to 127.0.0.1 (IPv4) or ::1 (IPv6), that is, from the server to itself, need a scram-sha-256 password. The three replication lines do the same for physical replication, which you will use in Part 33. Nothing allows a connection from another machine yet.

Above the first line Ubuntu writes "DO NOT DISABLE!". Keep local all postgres peer as the first rule. The packaging scripts and maintenance jobs log in as postgres through the socket without a password; if you change that line you must give the superuser another way in.
Step 3: See the same rules from SQL
On db1, as the postgres user through psql. The pg_hba_file_rules view parses the file and shows one row per rule. Only superusers can read it by default.

data.code:
SELECT rule_number, line_number, type, database, user_name, address, auth_method
  FROM pg_hba_file_rules;
data.caption: Parse pg_hba.conf from SQL

data.code:
rule_number | line_number | type  |   database    | user_name  |  address  |  auth_method  
-------------+-------------+-------+---------------+------------+-----------+---------------
           1 |         118 | local | {all}         | {postgres} |           | peer
           2 |         123 | local | {all}         | {all}      |           | peer
           3 |         125 | host  | {all}         | {all}      | 127.0.0.1 | scram-sha-256
           4 |         127 | host  | {all}         | {all}      | ::1       | scram-sha-256
           5 |         130 | local | {replication} | {all}      |           | peer
           6 |         131 | host  | {replication} | {all}      | 127.0.0.1 | scram-sha-256
           7 |         132 | host  | {replication} | {all}      | ::1       | scram-sha-256
(7 rows)
data.caption: Output

data.text: rule_number is the order the server checks rules in, and line_number tells you where to look in the file. This view reads the file as it is on disk now, not what the server last loaded. That makes it the perfect test before a reload, as you will see in Step 7.
Step 4: See peer authentication in action
On db1, as root or any Linux user that is not postgres. Try to connect as the database user postgres:

data.code: psql -U postgres -d postgres -c "SELECT 1;"
data.caption: Connect as postgres from another Linux user

data.code: psql: error: connection to server on socket "/var/run/postgresql/.s.PGSQL.5432" failed: FATAL:  Peer authentication failed for user "postgres"
data.caption: Output

data.text: Rule 1 matched (local, any database, user postgres) and its method is peer. The kernel reported the Linux user root, which is not postgres, so the server refused. This is why the series always uses sudo -u postgres psql: it runs psql as the Linux user postgres, and peer lets it in.
Letting an application server connect
A common job: the application on app1 (10.0.0.21) must reach database shop on db1 as user app_user with a password. The connection path looks like this:

data.code: app1 (10.0.0.21)  --TCP 5432, scram-sha-256-->  db1 (10.0.0.11:5432)  database shop, role app_user
data.caption: Connection path for this part

data.text: Step 5: Create the role and database
On db1, as the postgres user. A rule is useless if the role has no password: password methods always fail for a role whose stored password is null.

data.caption: Create a login role with a password and its database

data.code:
CREATE ROLE
CREATE DATABASE
 password_encryption 
---------------------
 scram-sha-256
(1 row)

 rolname  |   hash_start   
----------+----------------
 app_user | SCRAM-SHA-256$
(1 row)
data.caption: Output

data.text: password_encryption (default scram-sha-256) decides how a new password is hashed at the moment it is set. The stored value starts with SCRAM-SHA-256$, so this role can use scram-sha-256 authentication. In real life, set passwords with the psql meta-command \password app_user so the plain password never appears in your shell history or the server log.
Verify through the loopback rule (rule 3), from db1 itself:

data.code:
PGPASSWORD='Str0ng#Pass' psql -h 127.0.0.1 -U app_user -d shop \
  -c "SELECT current_user, inet_client_addr(), inet_server_addr();"
data.caption: Test a password login over TCP

content: Connect over TCP/IP to this host instead of the Unix socket, so a host rule is used
Database user name to connect as
Environment variable with the password, used here only to make the test non-interactive

data.text: Step 6: Make the server listen on the network

On db1, as your sudo user. By default listen_addresses is localhost, so the server does not even accept TCP connections from other machines. This setting can only be set at server start, so it needs a restart. Using a conf.d file, as in Part 5:

data.code:
# /etc/postgresql/18/main/conf.d/10-listen.conf
# before: not set (default listen_addresses = 'localhost')
# after:
listen_addresses = '*'
data.caption: New file /etc/postgresql/18/main/conf.d/10-listen.conf

data.code:
echo "listen_addresses = '*'" | sudo -u postgres tee /etc/postgresql/18/main/conf.d/10-listen.conf
sudo systemctl restart postgresql@18-main
sudo -u postgres psql -c "SHOW listen_addresses;"
data.caption: Listen on all interfaces and restart

data.code:
listen_addresses = '*'
 listen_addresses 
------------------
 *
(1 row)
data.caption: Output

data.text: * means all available IP interfaces. You can instead list specific addresses, for example 'localhost, 10.0.0.11', to listen only on the private network. Verify in the server log:

data.code: sudo grep 'listening on' /var/log/postgresql/postgresql-18-main.log | tail -2
data.caption: Check which addresses the server listens on

data.code:
2026-10-26 12:58:42.807 UTC [1485] LOG:  listening on IPv4 address "0.0.0.0", port 5432
2026-10-26 12:58:42.811 UTC [1485] LOG:  listening on Unix socket "/var/run/postgresql/.s.PGSQL.5432"
data.caption: Output (expected output: log file name for cluster 18 main; on a host with IPv6 you also see a line for "::")

data.text: If you only reload instead of restarting, the log says parameter "listen_addresses" cannot be changed without restarting the server and nothing changes. Undo: sudo rm /etc/postgresql/18/main/conf.d/10-listen.conf and restart again. Also allow port 5432 in any firewall (for example ufw) between app1 and db1, only from the app network.
Now try to connect to db1 through its network address. From db1 itself this uses the 10.0.0.11 interface, so the loopback rules do not match:

data.code: PGPASSWORD='Str0ng#Pass' psql -h 10.0.0.11 -U app_user -d shop -c "SELECT 1;"
data.caption: Connect through the network address

data.code:
psql: error: connection to server at "10.0.0.11", port 5432 failed: FATAL:  no pg_hba.conf entry for host "10.0.0.11", user "app_user", database "shop", SSL encryption
connection to server at "10.0.0.11", port 5432 failed: FATAL:  no pg_hba.conf entry for host "10.0.0.11", user "app_user", database "shop", no encryption
data.caption: Output (expected output: the address is your server's)

data.text: The server now listens, but no rule matches this address. psql tried twice because Ubuntu enables SSL by default: first with SSL encryption, then without. Neither matched any line, so the server refused both.
Step 7: Add the rule and test it before reloading
On db1, as your sudo user. Back up the file, then add the new rule at the end with an editor such as nano:

data.code:
sudo cp -p /etc/postgresql/18/main/pg_hba.conf /etc/postgresql/18/main/pg_hba.conf.bak
sudo nano /etc/postgresql/18/main/pg_hba.conf
data.caption: Back up and edit pg_hba.conf

data.code:
# before: the file ends with the "host replication all ::1/128 scram-sha-256" line
# after: these lines added at the end

# Application servers on the app network
host    shop            app_user        10.0.0.0/24             scram-sha-256
data.caption: Lines added to /etc/postgresql/18/main/pg_hba.conf

data.text: This rule allows only TCP connections, only to database shop, only as app_user, only from 10.0.0.0 to 10.0.0.255, and only with a SCRAM password. Keep rules this narrow; avoid host all all 0.0.0.0/0, which opens every database to the whole internet if the port is reachable.
Before you reload, ask the server to parse the file. Here is what you see if you made a typo, writing scram-sha256 without the second hyphen:

data.caption: Look for errors in pg_hba.conf

data.code:
line_number | auth_method |                    error                     
-------------+-------------+----------------------------------------------
         135 |             | invalid authentication method "scram-sha256"
(1 row)
data.caption: Output (with the typo)

data.text: If you reload with this error, the server logs the problem and keeps using the old rules. The connection still fails and only the log tells you why:

data.code:
LOG:  received SIGHUP, reloading configuration files
LOG:  invalid authentication method "scram-sha256"
CONTEXT:  line 135 of configuration file "/etc/postgresql/18/main/pg_hba.conf"
LOG:  /etc/postgresql/18/main/pg_hba.conf was not reloaded
data.caption: Server log after reloading a broken file (expected output: path for 18; timestamps removed)

data.text: Fix the typo and run the check again. When the query returns no rows, look at the new rule:

data.caption: Check the new rule
Output (expected output: address from the example network)

data.text: Step 8: Reload and verify
On db1, as your sudo user. pg_hba.conf needs only a reload:

data.code:
sudo systemctl reload postgresql@18-main
sudo tail -1 /var/log/postgresql/postgresql-18-main.log
data.caption: Reload the configuration

data.code: 2026-10-26 12:59:10.926 UTC [1485] LOG:  received SIGHUP, reloading configuration files
data.caption: Output

data.text: No "was not reloaded" line follows, so the new rules are active. SELECT pg_reload_conf(); as a superuser does the same thing. Verify from app1 (or from db1 with -h 10.0.0.11):

data.code:
PGPASSWORD='Str0ng#Pass' psql -h 10.0.0.11 -U app_user -d shop \
  -c "SELECT current_user, current_database(), inet_client_addr();"
data.caption: Connect through the new rule

data.code:
current_user | current_database | inet_client_addr 
--------------+------------------+------------------
 app_user     | shop             | 10.0.0.11
(1 row)
data.caption: Output (expected output: from app1 the client address is 10.0.0.21)

data.text: Now prove the rule is as narrow as you meant. The same user asking for another database is refused, because no line matches database postgres from this address:

data.code: psql: error: connection to server at "10.0.0.11", port 5432 failed: FATAL:  no pg_hba.conf entry for host "10.0.0.11", user "app_user", database "postgres", SSL encryption
data.caption: Output of the same command with -d postgres (expected output)

data.text: Undo: delete the two added lines (or sudo cp -p /etc/postgresql/18/main/pg_hba.conf.bak /etc/postgresql/18/main/pg_hba.conf) and reload.
Rule order: first match wins
Step 9: Block one user with a reject rule
On db1, as your sudo user. To see first-match in action, add a reject line above the IPv4 loopback rule, so it is checked first:

data.code:
# before:
# IPv4 local connections:
host    all             all             127.0.0.1/32            scram-sha-256

# after:
host    shop            app_user        127.0.0.1/32            reject
# IPv4 local connections:
host    all             all             127.0.0.1/32            scram-sha-256
data.caption: Edit in /etc/postgresql/18/main/pg_hba.conf

data.text: Check the order, then reload:

data.caption: Check rule order and reload

data.text: Verify with two connections from db1:

data.code:
PGPASSWORD='Str0ng#Pass' psql -h 127.0.0.1 -U app_user -d shop -c "SELECT 1;"
PGPASSWORD='Str0ng#Pass' psql -h 127.0.0.1 -U app_user -d postgres -c "SELECT current_user, current_database();"
data.caption: Test both databases

data.code:
psql: error: connection to server at "127.0.0.1", port 5432 failed: FATAL:  pg_hba.conf rejects connection for host "127.0.0.1", user "app_user", database "shop", SSL encryption
connection to server at "127.0.0.1", port 5432 failed: FATAL:  pg_hba.conf rejects connection for host "127.0.0.1", user "app_user", database "shop", no encryption
 current_user | current_database 
--------------+------------------
 app_user     | postgres
(1 row)
data.caption: Output

data.text: The correct password did not help for shop: rule 3 matched first and its method is reject, so the server never looked at rule 4. For database postgres, rule 3 does not match, so rule 4 applies and the password works. The lesson: put narrow rules first and broad rules last. A broad rule high in the file silently hides every rule below it.
Undo: delete the reject line and reload. Rule numbers return to what you saw in Step 3.
Moving from MD5 to SCRAM

PostgreSQL 18 deprecates MD5 passwords: support will be removed in a future major release. Servers upgraded from old versions often still have roles with MD5 hashes. An MD5 hash cannot be used with scram-sha-256, so those users fail to log in the day you switch the rules.
Step 10: Find roles with MD5 passwords
On db1, as the postgres user. To have something to find, create an old-style role. The SET changes password_encryption for this session only:

data.caption: Create a role with an MD5 password (test only)

data.text: On PostgreSQL 18 the CREATE ROLE prints a deprecation warning:

data.code:
WARNING:  setting an MD5-encrypted password
DETAIL:  MD5 password support is deprecated and will be removed in a future release of PostgreSQL.
HINT:  Refer to the PostgreSQL documentation for details about migrating to another password type.
CREATE ROLE
data.caption: Output (expected output on PostgreSQL 18)

data.text: You can turn this warning off with md5_password_warnings = off (new in PostgreSQL 18, default on), but it is better to fix the passwords. List every role whose stored hash is MD5:

data.caption: Find MD5 password hashes

data.code:
rolname   |   hash_start   
-------------+----------------
 legacy_user | md55804793cdf4
(1 row)
data.caption: Output

data.text: Step 11: Re-set the password and switch the rule

The documented order is: make sure every client library supports SCRAM, keep password_encryption = scram-sha-256 (the default), have each user set a new password, then change the method in pg_hba.conf from md5 to scram-sha-256. Re-set the password:

data.caption: Re-hash the password with SCRAM and verify

data.code:
ALTER ROLE
   rolname   |   hash_start   
-------------+----------------
 app_user    | SCRAM-SHA-256$
 legacy_user | SCRAM-SHA-256$
(2 rows)
data.caption: Output

data.text: While you migrate, a line with method md5 still works for users who already have SCRAM hashes: the server automatically uses SCRAM for them. That lets you convert users one by one and change md5 to scram-sha-256 in pg_hba.conf at the end, followed by a reload. Cleanup:

data.code: sudo -u postgres psql -c "DROP ROLE legacy_user;"
data.caption: Remove the test role

data.text: Common mistakes and how to fix them
FATAL: no pg_hba.conf entry for host "...", user "...", database "...", no encryption

No line matches this combination of type, address, database and user. Copy the three values from the message and compare them with pg_hba_file_rules. Usual causes: the client address is outside the CIDR range, the database name is different (if the client gives no database, it defaults to the user name), or you edited the file but did not reload. The words "SSL encryption" or "no encryption" tell you which attempt was refused; a hostssl line never matches a non-SSL attempt.
FATAL: pg_hba.conf rejects connection for host "..."
A reject line matched first. Find it in pg_hba_file_rules, then move your allow rule above it or narrow the reject rule.
FATAL: password authentication failed for user "..."

A line matched and asked for a password, but the check failed. The client sees the same message for a wrong password, a role with no password and a role that does not exist. The server log has the real reason and the matching line:

data.code:
FATAL:  password authentication failed for user "no_pw_user"
DETAIL:  User "no_pw_user" has no password assigned.
	Connection matched file "/etc/postgresql/18/main/pg_hba.conf" line 125: "host    all             all             127.0.0.1/32            scram-sha-256"
data.caption: Server log (expected output: path for 18)

data.text: Other DETAIL lines you will see are Role "ghost" does not exist. and, for a role that still has an MD5 hash on a scram-sha-256 line, User "legacy_user" does not have a valid SCRAM secret.. Fix: \password username in psql as a superuser. Find login roles without a password with SELECT rolname FROM pg_authid WHERE rolcanlogin AND rolpassword IS NULL; (postgres appears there by design: it logs in with peer).
FATAL: Peer authentication failed for user "postgres"
You ran psql -U postgres as a Linux user that is not postgres. Use sudo -u postgres psql. Do not "fix" this by changing peer to trust.
Connection refused or timeout from another machine

If the error says connection refused or times out instead of a FATAL message, the client never reached the server. Check listen_addresses (and that you restarted), and the firewall. pg_hba.conf is checked only after the TCP connection succeeds.
Edited the file but nothing changed
You did not reload, or the reload failed. Search the log for was not reloaded and query pg_hba_file_rules for errors.

Never put trust on a host line in production, even "just for a minute" to recover a password. Anyone who can reach the port can then connect as any user, including postgres. To reset a lost password, use sudo -u postgres psql through the existing peer rule and run \password.
Practice exercise

items.content: Create a role report_user with a password and allow it to connect only to database shop, only from the single address 10.0.0.30, with scram-sha-256. Check the rule with pg_hba_file_rules before you reload.
Write the same rule by mistake as 10.0.0.30/24, query pg_hba_file_rules, and look at the error, address and netmask columns. Which clients does this line really allow? Then fix it.

data.title: Answer
data.text: Answer: CREATE ROLE report_user LOGIN PASSWORD '...'; then add host shop report_user 10.0.0.30/32 scram-sha-256 and run SELECT pg_reload_conf();. For task 2, the error column is empty: the file loads without complaint, and the view shows address 10.0.0.30 with netmask 255.255.255.0. The server compares only the first 24 bits, so the line allows the whole 10.0.0.x network. Always use /32 for one IPv4 host and check the netmask column.
Quick reference

data.code:
# Where is pg_hba.conf?
sudo -u postgres psql -c "SHOW hba_file;"

# Show the active rules without comments
sudo grep -vE '^\s*(#|$)' /etc/postgresql/18/main/pg_hba.conf

# Parse the file from SQL (on-disk contents, before reload)
sudo -u postgres psql -c "SELECT rule_number, line_number, type, database, user_name, address, auth_method, error FROM pg_hba_file_rules;"

# Create a role with a SCRAM password and its database
sudo -u postgres psql -c "CREATE ROLE app_user LOGIN PASSWORD 'Str0ng#Pass';"
sudo -u postgres psql -c "CREATE DATABASE shop OWNER app_user;"

# Listen on the network (restart needed)
echo "listen_addresses = '*'" | sudo -u postgres tee /etc/postgresql/18/main/conf.d/10-listen.conf
sudo systemctl restart postgresql@18-main

# Back up and edit pg_hba.conf, add:
#   host  shop  app_user  10.0.0.0/24  scram-sha-256
sudo cp -p /etc/postgresql/18/main/pg_hba.conf /etc/postgresql/18/main/pg_hba.conf.bak
sudo nano /etc/postgresql/18/main/pg_hba.conf

# Check for errors before reloading
sudo -u postgres psql -c "SELECT line_number, error FROM pg_hba_file_rules WHERE error IS NOT NULL;"

# Reload and check the log
sudo systemctl reload postgresql@18-main
sudo tail -3 /var/log/postgresql/postgresql-18-main.log

# Test a connection over TCP
psql -h 10.0.0.11 -U app_user -d shop -c "SELECT current_user, inet_client_addr();"

# Find roles still using MD5 hashes
sudo -u postgres psql -c "SELECT rolname FROM pg_authid WHERE rolpassword LIKE 'md5%';"

data.text: Summary and what's next

items.content: pg_hba.conf decides who may connect, to which database, from where, and with which method; on Ubuntu it is /etc/postgresql/18/main/pg_hba.conf
The first matching line wins, and there is no fall-through: narrow rules go first
Use peer for local admin access and scram-sha-256 for passwords; never trust on network lines
Remote access needs listen_addresses (restart) plus a host rule (reload)
Test with pg_hba_file_rules before every reload; a broken file is not loaded
Find MD5 hashes in pg_authid and re-set those passwords, since PostgreSQL 18 deprecates MD5
When a login fails, read the server log: it names the reason and the matching line

data.text: In Part 7 you will learn roles, users, groups and privileges: GRANT, REVOKE and default privileges.

linkedin.post:
A correct password can still be refused by PostgreSQL. The reason is almost always one line in pg_hba.conf.

Part 6 of my PostgreSQL DBA series is about client authentication. What to know:

→ The first matching line wins. If it fails, PostgreSQL does not try the next one. Put narrow rules first.
→ Remote access needs two changes: listen_addresses = '*' (restart) and a host line in pg_hba.conf (reload).
→ Test before you reload: SELECT line_number, error FROM pg_hba_file_rules WHERE error IS NOT NULL;
→ A broken file is not loaded at all. The log says "pg_hba.conf was not reloaded" and the old rules stay.
→ PostgreSQL 18 deprecates MD5 passwords. Find them with WHERE rolpassword LIKE 'md5%' and re-set them so they are stored as SCRAM.

Every step is tested on Ubuntu with PostgreSQL 18, with real output and the exact error messages.

Which authentication error has cost you the most time: "no pg_hba.conf entry" or "password authentication failed"?

Follow along for Part 7: roles and privileges.
